_note: JSON sidecar for migration-manifest.yaml. The wizard runtime CLI consumes JSON; YAML is the human-facing companion. Both files MUST stay in sync.

agents/lib/external_write/acceptance_rep.benefit: New file. Gives you a sanctioned way to mark a recorded acceptance repudiated. Doing so switches that capability back off and queues it for a fresh trial: a repudiation that left live permission standing would be worse than none at all.

agents/lib/external_write/adapters_gmail.benefit: Records, for each kind of operation this adapter performs, whether its undo puts things back to an exact earlier state. Two kinds are declared and one is deliberately left undeclared, with the reason written next to it: leaving it undeclared means it is refused a trial, which is the safe outcome, and declaring it falsely would be a false statement at the point that authorises a real write.

agents/lib/external_write/capability_hea.benefit: The health view now takes account of a wrapper whose guard has stopped a scheduled run, and continues to withhold the all-clear while anything at all is outstanding.

agents/lib/external_write/command_manife.benefit: Registers the new trial command as one that writes to your outside system, so it is never eligible for automatic approval and always requires you.

agents/lib/external_write/copy_run_proof.benefit: The location of a capability's proof file is now built in one place and used by both the side that writes it and the side that reads it, so a proof cannot be written somewhere acceptance does not look.

agents/lib/external_write/operator_accep.benefit: Which states allow you to acknowledge a risk is now an explicit list of the states that qualify, instead of a list of the ones that do not. A state added later therefore cannot become acknowledgeable just by not being excluded.

agents/lib/external_write/scan.py.benefit: Adds two build-time checks. One flags a file that hard-codes your own confirmation instead of asking you. The other flags a repair instruction written by hand into the surface that displays it, rather than coming from the single place those instructions are defined -- which is how two surfaces came to tell you different things about the same problem.

agents/lib/external_write/state_actions..benefit: New file. A single list pairing every state that holds something up with the exact instruction and command that clears it, plus a companion list naming, in plain language, the states that deliberately need no action. A state in neither list fails the build, so 'nothing to do here' has to be a written decision rather than an omission.

agents/lib/external_write/suppressed_inv.benefit: New file. Records the moment a paused wrapper's guard stops a scheduled run, so a job that has quietly stopped producing output becomes visible. This records the guard STOPPING a run; it does not detect a guard that fails to stop one.

agents/lib/external_write/trial_eligibil.benefit: New file. Decides whether one operation may be trialled at all, from what its adapter declares about itself. Anything it cannot establish is refused rather than allowed: an operation that says nothing about whether its undo restores an exact earlier state does not become eligible by staying silent.

agents/lib/external_write/trial_executor.benefit: New file. Runs the trial and produces the proof that switching a capability on asks for. This is the piece you can invoke. Before it existed, that proof had no producer you could run, which is why a capability could be set up correctly and never become switchable.

agents/lib/external_write/trial_journal..benefit: New file. Writes down what a trial is about to do and flushes it to disk -- the file and the folder holding it -- before the change is attempted. If the run is interrupted at any moment, the record of what was in flight is on disk and can be found again.

agents/lib/external_write/trial_recovery.benefit: New file. The one place a unit left needing recovery can be cleared, and only after the system has looked at the state the unit was actually left in rather than assuming it.

agents/lib/external_write/write_authoriz.benefit: New file. Holds the single decision about whether an operation is allowed to run, so a trial run and an ordinary run are checked by the same code rather than by two copies that have to agree with each other. Nothing about what is allowed was relaxed to make the trial possible.

agents/lib/external_write/write_gate.py.benefit: Adds a read-only accessor so a caller that needs to know which route an operation will actually take asks the gate rather than working it out a second way. Nothing about what the gate permits changed.

agents/lib/external_write/writer_ack_sto.benefit: New file. The store for your recorded risk acknowledgements, separated out as part of the same layering. No change on its own to what your system does.

agents/lib/external_write/writer_command.benefit: New file. The commands offered for writer states, separated out as part of the same layering. No change on its own to what your system does.

agents/lib/external_write/writer_state_c.benefit: New file. Part of splitting the writer-state code into layers that no longer import each other in a circle. No change on its own to what your system does; it is what makes the state-to-action list above possible to build.

agents/lib/external_write/zones.py.benefit: Records the new files above in the list of files that are part of the safe-write core itself, rather than capability code. No change to what any capability may do.

migrations.migration_steps: 1. Run the update check (it reports what's new + the recommendation). 2. On the operator's yes, the assistant applies it ("${{WIZARD_HOME:-$HOME/agent-wizard}}/scripts/wizard" self-upgrade --to v0.23.0 --apply). 3. A backup is taken first; the operator's own data, rules, credentials, and logs are never touched.
migrations.notes: Minor-additive release to v0.23.0. This release closes two situations in which your system could reach a state it could describe to you but you had no way to leave. FIRST: switching a capability on has always required a proof that it can make its change on the real system and put it back. Until now nothing you could run produced that proof, so a capability could be set up correctly and still never become switchable. You can now run a single trial of one operation. It goes through exactly the same safety gates a live run goes through -- the same limit on how much it may touch, the same record of what it did -- and what it is about to do is written and flushed to disk before the change is attempted, so a run that is interrupted at any moment leaves a record that can be found again. A trial that completes produces the proof that acceptance asks for. SECOND: every state that holds something up now names, in one place, the exact instruction and command that clears it, or is written down in plain language as needing no action; a state that is in neither list now fails the build instead of shipping silently. A unit left needing recovery can be cleared, and only after the system has looked at the state it was actually left in. ALSO IN THIS RELEASE: acknowledging a risk is now limited to an explicit list of the states that qualify, so a state added later cannot become acknowledgeable simply by not being excluded. You can now mark a recorded acceptance repudiated -- that switches the capability back off and queues it for a fresh trial, rather than leaving live permission standing behind a record you no longer trust. A paused wrapper now records the moment its guard stops a scheduled run, so a job that has quietly stopped producing output becomes visible instead of staying silent. And two new build-time checks were added: one flags a script that hard-codes your own confirmation, and one flags a repair instruction hand-written into the surface that displays it instead of coming from the single place those instructions are defined. DECLARED, NOT PROVEN -- said in these words on purpose: whether an adapter's undo is safe to repeat is a declaration the system reads, not a property it can verify; recovery may issue a write that changes nothing, because restoring a value to what it already is remains a real call to the outside service; and the upgrade step that adds the new undo declaration to an adapter you or your assistant wrote sets it to the SAFE value, never to yes -- only a person, or an assistant that has read the code, may change it. STILL OPEN, named rather than implied fixed: a retrial item's next step exists on disk and in the skills but is not printed by any surface; a paused hand-rolled writer's pair of marker files has a written route out but no single command that performs it; and a wrapper's guard is recognised by what it looks like, which does not establish that it will fire. No breaking changes; all existing capabilities and files are unaffected.
migrations.preflight: Verify the operator project carries a .wizard/manifest.json whose foundation_bundle_version is v0.22.0 (or any version in the supported range). A backup is taken automatically.
migrations.rollback: Restore from .wizard/backups/pre-v0.23.0/ and set foundation_bundle_version back to v0.22.0.

On the operator's yes, the assistant applies it ("${{WIZARD_HOME:-$HOME/agent-wizard}}/scripts/wizard" self-upgrade --to v0.23.0 --apply). 3. A backup is taken first; the operator's own data, rules, credentials, and logs are never touched.
migrations.notes: Minor-additive release to v0.23.0. This release closes two situations in which your system could reach a state it could describe to you but you had no way to leave. FIRST: switching a capability on has always required a proof that it can make its change on the real system and put it back. Until now nothing you could run produced that proof, so a capability could be set up correctly and still never become switchable. You can now run a single trial of one operation. It goes through exactly the same safety gates a live run goes through -- the same limit on how much it may touch, the same record of what it did -- and what it is about to do is written and flushed to disk before the change is attempted, so a run that is interrupted at any moment leaves a record that can be found again. A trial that completes produces the proof that acceptance asks for. SECOND: every state that holds something up now names, in one place, the exact instruction and command that clears it, or is written down in plain language as needing no action; a state that is in neither list now fails the build instead of shipping silently. A unit left needing recovery can be cleared, and only after the system has looked at the state it was actually left in. ALSO IN THIS RELEASE: acknowledging a risk is now limited to an explicit list of the states that qualify, so a state added later cannot become acknowledgeable simply by not being excluded. You can now mark a recorded acceptance repudiated -- that switches the capability back off and queues it for a fresh trial, rather than leaving live permission standing behind a record you no longer trust. A paused wrapper now records the moment its guard stops a scheduled run, so a job that has quietly stopped producing output becomes visible instead of staying silent. And two new build-time checks were added: one flags a script that hard-codes your own confirmation, and one flags a repair instruction hand-written into the surface that displays it instead of coming from the single place those instructions are defined. DECLARED, NOT PROVEN -- said in these words on purpose: whether an adapter's undo is safe to repeat is a declaration the system reads, not a property it can verify; recovery may issue a write that changes nothing, because restoring a value to what it already is remains a real call to the outside service; and the upgrade step that adds the new undo declaration to an adapter you or your assistant wrote sets it to the SAFE value, never to yes -- only a person, or an assistant that has read the code, may change it. STILL OPEN, named rather than implied fixed: a retrial item's next step exists on disk and in the skills but is not printed by any surface; a paused hand-rolled writer's pair of marker files has a written route out but no single command that performs it; and a wrapper's guard is recognised by what it looks like, which does not establish that it will fire. No breaking changes; all existing capabilities and files are unaffected.
